title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
The skills acquired in this lab class are crucial for bioinformatic tasks using molecular data, such as data analysis, scripting, and working in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. My hope is that you don’t just type the commands into the terminal and move on – I would like you to think about what these commands are doing and start imagining how they could be useful in analyzing your own data.


Each lab is inteded to be a reference point for you on various bioinformatic tasks. To make the most of these labs, please treat them like a personal resource, so adjust any specific commands accordingly.

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Preparing today’s lab
Today, we will working with the transcript quantification data prepared in the last lab, which used the previously published Drosophila melanogaster data.
If you have not already, you should make a folder on your Desktop for today’s lab. You can name this anything you want (I am going to call mine DGE_Analysis)

Open two terminal windows.
In one of those terminals, log onto the HPC
On the HPC and in your lab folder in scr10, you should move into your transcript_quantification folder
cd scr10/BIOL_404L/transcript_quantification/
Use pwd to view the PATH to this folder. Make sure to copy this path!
Using your local terminal (not connected to the HPC), move into today’s folder (again, I called mine DGE_Analysis)
 cd Desktop/coding/BIOL 404L/Guided_DGE_Data/
You will use your local terminal (not connected to the HPC) to download the data from the Salmon_Quant folder.
scp -r cwwang@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:/sciclone/home/cwwang/scr10/BIOL_404L/transcript_quantification/Salmon_Quant ./
scp works by moving files from a location to another location.
By putting the files from the HPC first, scp will copy those files from the HPC to your computer.
Once your local terminal says the files have downloaded, you can close the terminal connected to the HPC. Do not close your local terminal yet!

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Preparing R-Studio
Today, we will be using DESeq2 to perform the differential gene expression, which is a fantastic tool built for R. To use it though, we will need to install some R packages to make sure it works.
To make life easy, I recommend making a new R-script to save today’s commands. This will make a great reference point for yourself in the future!

We have a number of tools to install in R. Fortunately, this is very easy with the install.packages() command. Like conda, there is a special package manager for R that handles biology-related tools, called Bioconductor. We will install this first as it will manage the installs for the remaining R packages.
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
 install.packages("BiocManager")
For the remaining software, I will provide you with one install command, and you will have to install the remaining software in the list that follows. You will likely be prompted to update things when trying to install the additional software. When that happens just update all the packages, a.
BiocManager::install("tximport")

readr
DESeq2
apeglm
txdbmaker
AnnotationDbi
pheatmap


Note that you will only need to install the software ONE time!

Now that everything is installed, we need to “import” those tools. Again, I will provide a single example, and you should go ahead and repeat it for all the tools installed.
library("tximport")

Great, now the tools for R are all loaded and prepared! We now need to do a little more preparation before we can do the analysis itself.

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Trasncript-to-Gene-Name Table
While Salmon quantifies expression based on transcripts, we tend to want to explore gene-level expression instead, which is what we will be doing! It does make the interpretation a bit more simple, but it also means that we need to prepare the transcript-to-gene table.
Fortunately, we just need the .gtf file, which can be downloaded from Blackboard.
Below, are the steps to prepare this table.

You will create the transcript-db table from the Drosophila.Genome.gtf file. To do this, you will need the PATH to this file. This is pretty easy to do!
Find this file on your computer, then drag it into your terminal! You should see the file’s PATH.
Make sure to copy this path!
We can put this PATH into R-Studio
txdb <- makeTxDbFromGFF(file = "PATH-TO-GTF-FILE", format = "gtf")
Now we need to extract the transcript names
k <- keys(txdb, keytype = "TXNAME")
Now we can pair each transcript name with its corresponding gene ID. Remember, all gene ID’s are unique and may have multiple transcripts (isoforms) corresponding to them. We want to “flatten” this to make it easier to analyze.
tx2gene <- select(txdb, keys = k, columns = "GENEID", keytype = "TXNAME")
R is fantastic, because it makes it easy to see the data as well. We can check out the first few rows of this transcript-to-gene table using head()
head(tx2gene)
While we can move on with the remaining preparation steps and analysis, it is always a good idea to save these types of tables, just in case. We will save the table in the same place as the DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv file, to keep them together.

Copy the PATH to the DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv, excluding the filename! We just want the folder location.

Using the PATH you copied, let’s save the table.
write.csv(tx2gene, file = "/Users/colinwang/Desktop/coding/BIOL\ 404L/Guided_DGE_Data/dmel.tx2gene", row.names = FALSE)

Now we just need to update the meta-data table and we are nearly set!

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Preparing the Meta-Data Table
To make life as easy as possible, we are going to add a little more information to the DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv file. In fact, we are going to link each sample (row) in the table to the PATH to the corresponding transcript quantification output file (quant.sf) generated by Salmon.

In your local terminal, navigate to the folder that has all of your folders generated by Salmon. Mine are in the Salmon_Quant folder still.
cd /Users/colinwang/Desktop/coding/BIOL\ 404L/Guided_DGE_Data/Salmon_Quant/
In the DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv file, make a new column called quant_folders. Each row will need you to paste the folder that the Salmon output folders are in, as well as the folder for that specific replicate.
For me, the very first sample would be Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant



Example of the prepared metadata for my computer



At this point, your folder with all the relevant data should look something like this:

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Putting Everything Together
We are finally prepared to run the differential gene expression analysis! Well, almost ready. The steps below are predominantly for R and will let you know explicitly when you need to access the terminal.

Using your terminal (right away, ha!), find and copy the path to your DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv file.
/Users/colinwang/Desktop/coding/BIOL\ 404L/Guided_DGE_Data/DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv 
In your R script, we need to make a variable, dir, that has the PATH to your folder. This should be the same as the path you copied above, just removing the file.
dir <- "/Users/colinwang/Desktop/coding/BIOL\ 404L/Guided_DGE_Data/"
Next is to make another variable, samples. We will pass it the location of the DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv file, which has all of the information for the analysis.
samples <- read.csv(file.path(dir, "DGE.Drosophila.Metadata.csv"))
read.csv(): tells the code to read a comma-separated-values file file.path(): tells R to find the path to the file located in a specific directory When combined (as in the command above) it finds the table, reads it, and saves its contents to samples
Let’s look at the first few lines of samples, using head()
head(samples)

You should see all the meta-data that we need!
Now we need to tell R where the quant.sf files are in our folder. We will save those locations to another variable, quant_files
quant_files <- file.path(dir, samples$quant_folder, "quant.sf")
Also, it’s a good time to use head to just check that everything looks right too!
head(quant_files)
Now, we need to link the quant.sf files to the tx2gene data we prepared. This also serves as an opportunity to tell R that the data were generated using Salmon

txi <- tximport(quant_files, type = "salmon", tx2gene = tx2gene)

We are at a critical part in preparing our data for DESeq2. Many experiments are designed to be relatively simple, such as untreated versus treated. However, our data have two big variables to test that could impact our analyses: temperature and location.
It could be that the predominant difference in gene expression is driven by one of these factors. Although it is more likely that it is a combination of temperature and location. We need to tell DESeq2 that there may be an interaction between these variables.
DESeq2 by default knows nothing, and so the very last step towards preparing data for the analysis is to describe the experiment.
For our data, given that it is “multi-factor” and that the differentially expressed genes may be a result of the interaction between temperature and location, we will make sure our design reflects that.
To make the downstream work easier, we are going to explicitly make “groups” following our meta-data table. This will make it possible to make our broad comparisons more easily.
Let’s go ahead and explicitly describe our groups
samples$group <- factor(paste(samples$Geographic.Location, samples$Temperature, sep = "_"))
samples$group
You should see that each sample is similarly named to our metadata, with the geographic location AND the temperature!
Finally, we can prepare
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromTximport(txi, colData = samples, design = ~ group)






DESeq2’s design



The design argument in DESeq2 tells the software what variables could be contributing to the observed differential gene expression.
While we are using a multi-factor design, much of the time, research is just exploring a single variable (we will call it sample_type for this example), with multiple conditions (e.g., control, treatment-1, treatment-2):
design = ~ sample_type
DESeq2 has an amazing manual with some examples for other designs, so check there for more!

title: Differential Gene Expression
text:
Quality Checking BEFORE DGE!
Before we run our differential gene expression analysis, it is always nice to explore your data ahead of time. The focus here is to know if any of your samples are behaving unexpectedly, which could reflect a technical issue or some biological chaos!
From experience, there is the occassional mis-labeling of a sample, which can make the analysis challenging or impossible. Personally, if we are seeing that there is a strong likelihood that a sample is mis-labelled, you really have two options: 1) keep the mis-labelled sample as it is (personal preference) or 2) remove it from the study. Be aware that this does happen, and I recommend the most conservative (i.e., careful) approach is the “best” approach.
Alright, let’s dive in!

Let’s take a look at the actual data that we prepared for DESeq2
View(counts(dds))
In this table you will notice that there are 12 samples (columns) and many rows (genes). The values are the read “counts” generated by Salmon



Snippet of the dds table


Before we visualize the data, we are going to normalize the read counts to improve the data visualization steps. This is not always necessary, but it often makes for more appropriate comparisons. We will be using the regularized-logarithm transformation that is part of the DESeq2 package.
It is important to note that DESeq2 will use the raw read counts for the actual analysis, so do not pass the normalized values.
rld = rlog(dds, blind = TRUE)

blind: makes sure that rlog only looks at the counts and ignores all the other metadata!

Now we can run the principal components analysis, which a dimension reduction technique to visualize complex datasets in 2-D (i.e. graphs!). We will talk about how this works in class!
plotPCA(rld, intgroup = 'Temperature')

intgroup: provide a variable to distinguish your groups!

Go ahead and try replacing Temperature with Geographic.Location.
What do you notice?
The axis labels describe the variance in the dataset. In this dataset, the x-axis (PC1) and y-axis (PC2) account for 46% abd 18% of the variance, respectively. What is cool is that you can simply sum those values to get an idea of how much variability in your data are explained by these two axes, which is ~64% (this is pretty high!)
So cool!
Did you know that you can run the plotPCA with two variables to put on the plot?
plotPCA(rld, intgroup = c('Temperature', 'Geographic.Location'))
How cool is this? (very very cool)
In your plots you should notice that there is reasonable distance between each temperature and location! That’s a pretty nice dataset even without any data cleaning!



PCA plot of Geography and Temperature


The only other exploratory analysis we will do is some hierarchical clustering. Before we do this, we do need to extract some information from our big samples dataframe. This will make the visualization easier.
meta <- data.frame(samples$Temperature, samples$Geographic.Location, row.names = colnames(txi$counts))
We are just linking the variables we are testing to the samples themselves
Hierarchical clustering can be done many ways, but for today, we will simply explore the correlation between our raw samples. It is pretty straightforward to generate the pairwise correlation matrix
# converts the dataframe to a matrix
rld_mat <- assay(rld)

# generates the pairwise correlation matrix from the raw matrix
rld_corr <- cor(rld_mat)
Now we can do the visualization, using pheatmap. All this will need is our correlation matrix and our mini-metadata table.
pheatmap(rld_corr, annotation = meta)
What do you notice?
Interestingly, there is a clear separation of the data by temperature (whew). You might also notice that in the samples from 21C that one of the Panama samples is next to the Maine samples. This is a bit surprising, but I would not worry too much!
With correlation values so high (>0.99) there really are no outlier samples that we need to worry about.



Correlation heatmap looks pretty good!



The data look ready for our analysis!

title: DGE Vizualizations and Follow-up
text:
Installing the necessary R packages
Following last week’s steps for installations, we need to install a few more packages for today.
Using BiocManager, install: - [ ] clusterProfiler - [ ] AnnotationHub - [ ] ashr
We also need to install a few “normal” packages that may not be pre-installed yet - [ ] ggplot2 - [ ] dplyr - [ ] RColorBrewer - [ ] tibble - [ ] tidyr - [ ] scales
Once installed, make sure to load the libraries too! You can follow the example below
library(ggplot2)

title: DGE Vizualizations and Follow-up
text:
Preparing today’s lab
Today, we will re-work some of our differential gene expression analyses from last week. There are two reasons for this: 1) practice! and 2) there is a more appropriate means to shrink the log2-fold change. We were using apeglm, but for multi-factor designs, we ought to be using ashr instead.
To prepare for the lab, we will start with re-“shrinking” your differential gene expression data!
Following last week’s lab, we removed rows (genes) with minimal numbers of reads found in the entire row.

Make sure to remove the rows from your dds (DESeq2 dataset), following last week’s example
good_rows <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
dds <- dds[good_rows,]
Now we are going to explicitly set the “base” comparison that we want to run. Think of this as the control value. In our dataset, there is no explicit control. This means that we need to pick a reference point, and I think the Maine 21C fits that perfectly!
So we will “relevel” our dataset accordingly.
dds$group <- relevel(dds$group, ref = "Maine_21C")
dds <- DESeq(dds)
Now let’s check for the differentially expressed genes in our dataset! Do recall that this is inherently a pairwise comparison. I do think it is important to decide which comparisons will actually make sense.
Let’s start with the high and low temperature Maine samples!
result_maine_21C_29C_ashr <- lfcShrink(dds, contrast=c("group", "Maine_29C", "Maine_21C"), type = 'ashr', alpha = 0.05)

summary(result_maine_21C_29C_ashr)







Cautionary Note



If you compare the summary() of the two different lfcshrink methods, you will notice quite a substantial difference in the number of DGE’s that are inferred!
This is totally normal and expected.
apeglm is the recommended approach by the DESeq2 authors, in part because it is very aggressive in its “shrinking”. However, it does not handle interactions as well.
Remember interactions are tricky and are found in many datasets. In our example, there is likely an interaction between geographic locaiton and response to stress. Most Mainers would tell you that 21C is already a pretty warm day, with 29C being a rare heatwave day (or it used to be), whereas 21C would be quite cold for Panama.
This is an interaction that apeglm would be less good at tackling. That’s where ashr comes in, as it handles multi-factor designs and interactions very well!
At the end of the day, it is your choice, but it should be an informed choice!


We are ready to visualize our data!

title: DGE Vizualizations and Follow-up
text:
Visualizing DGE datasets with R
Below are just some examples on how to prepare some reasonable visualizations for differential gene expression datasets, using R. I do want to mention that while this lab course does use R, I am by no means an expert (I’m definitely a fan of python almost any task). View this section as a reasonable guide on how to do some fundamental visualizations.
As you explore your own datasets in this class, think about what sorts of visualizations are impactful and what you may like to see. We can work on these together in following sessions!
Ready to dive in?

We have built and linked our dataset names into our metadata table, but we can still make this better! We are going to make a new column, with the names being the geographyic location, temperature, and replicate (e.g., Maine_21C_1)
samples$sample_name <- paste(samples$Geographic.Location, samples$Temperature, samples$Replicate, sep = "_")
Typically, the dds dataframe has unlabeled columns, but we want to make sure to link the columns to the sample those data represent
colnames(dds) <- samples$sample_name
Now let’s normalize the read counts, while updating the column names to be easier to follow. You will see %>%, which simply is the R version of the |. In your terminal | is known as a “pipe” character. It implies the the output of a task is passed along to the next task, where the first task is to the left of the | character. R allows us to do this too!
normalized_counts <- counts(dds, normalized=T) %>%
 data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var="gene") %>%
  as_tibble()

We are saving a lot of steps into the normalized_counts variable. First, we are generating a table of normalized counts. Then, using %>%, we are taking those normalized counts, and converting them to a data-frame format. Afterwards, we are renaming the rows to match their gene names. Finally, we are saving it in a tibble format, which makes pretty tables.
A lot done in one small command! This is really cool and a common part of many bioinformatic pipelines.

Go ahead and use head to look at the top few rows of the normalized_counts table!
head(normalized_counts)
We are about to build our heatmap! It is not a bad plan to pick out which color palette to use. I am a huge fan of cold-warm (blue-red), but there are so many to play with! We can specify the number of colors to be in our palette too!
heat_colors <- rev(brewer.pal(6, "RdYlBu"))
Now let’s make our heatmap, it’s going to be intense!
pheatmap(normalized_counts[2:13],
      color = heat_colors,
      cluster_rows = T,
      cluster_cols = T,
      show_rownames = F,
      border_color = NA,
      fontsize = 10,
      scale = "row",
      treeheight_row = 0,
      height = 20)
There is a lot in this command! We will talk about slicing in the lecture, but that’s what we are doing with our normalized_counts table! We are generating a heatmap for columns 2-13, which correspond to our 12 samples!

cluster_rows = T :: cluster the rows (genes) by their expression patterns
cluster_cols = T :: cluster the columns (samples) by their expression patterns
show_rownames = F :: do not label all 10,000+ rows … that would be too much
border_color = NA :: do not put a border around the figure
fontsize = 10 :: font size (pretty self-explanatory)
scale = “row” :: applies a z-score normalization (makes comparisons within the row easier to interpret, by accounting for magnitude differences)
treeheight_row = 0 :: remove the ridiculous dendrogram on the rows
height = 20 :: size of the figure

Whew, this sure looks complicated!
Feel free to interactively save these plots. I almost always do all my “additions” to these plots using other tools (Inkscape is great, free, and does everything Adobe Illustrator can do!).
Now let’s make a volcano plot! This is inherently pairwise, so we will use the result_maine_21C_29C_ashr data we already prepared today. First, we will update this table by adding gene as the first column header.
res_df <- as.data.frame(result_maine_21C_29C_ashr) %>%
   tibble::rownames_to_column("gene")
Now we need to clean our data a bit. We will start by removing any rows (genes) missing adjusted p-values. This should not remove any rows, but it is important to double check
res_df <- res_df %>% filter(!is.na(padj))
Now let’s define our significance thresholds! If a gene has a log2fold change of at least 1 and an adjusted p-value < 0.05, it will be labeled “UP” regulated. If log2-fold change is less than -1 and an adjusted p-value < 0.05 then it will be labeled “DOWN” regulated. Otherwise, it is labeled as “NOT” having a difference.
res_df <- res_df %>%
  mutate(diffexpressed = case_when(
  log2FoldChange > 1 & padj < 0.05 ~ "UP",
  log2FoldChange < -1 & padj < 0.05 ~ "DOWN",
  TRUE ~ "NOT"
))

head(res_df)
Now we can make the plot! This command is frustratingly big. I will do my best to explain what is going on! Check the comments that are in the same line as each command. In this large plotting command, we use + to add another step in preparing our figure!
ggplot(res_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = diffexpressed)) + # plots the points and colors them based on their "type" of expression
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) + xlim(-2, 2) + # defines the size and opacity (alpha) of the points. alpha is NOT the p-value
  scale_color_manual(values = c("DOWN" = "blue", "NOT" = "grey", "UP" = "red")) + # manually setting the colors for our DEGs
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") + # makes the x-axis log2-fold change lines at x = -1 and x = 1
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") + # makes the y-axis adjusted p-value line
  theme_minimal() + # keeps the plot less crowded
  labs(x = "log2 Fold Change",
       y = "-log10 Adjusted p-value",
       color = "Expression") # labeles the axes and legend

It is always a fantastic idea to backup your comparisons and the normalized counts tables. This way it is easy to get to and reload instead of having to re-do the analyses each time you want to interact with your data.
So let’s save those tables.
write.csv(result_maine_21C_29C_ashr, file.path(dir, "Maine_21C_29C.DGE.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

write.csv(normalized_counts, file.path(dir, "Dmel_NormCounts.DGE.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

save(dds, file = file.path(dir, "Dmel.DDS.rda"))

title: DGE Vizualizations and Follow-up
text:
Gene Ontology Enrichment Analyses
So far we have visualized our differential gene expression dataset, but we really need to still figure out what the different in gene functions may be between our samples! This is exactly what Gene Ontology Enrichment Analyses are for!

If you have not already, load the AnnotationHub and clusterProfiler tools
We are exceedingly fortunate that we do not need to do any extra work to prepare GO annotations for Drosophila. Instead, the GO terms are already prepared and we just need to provide some details to clusterProfiler for our analyses.
Let’s use AnnotationHub to find the data for Drosophila.
First, we need to “initialize” AnnotationHub
ah <- AnnotationHub()
Now we can search for Drosophila
query(ah, c("Drosophila melanogaster", "OrgDb"))
You will notice that at the bottom of the output is the line: retrieve record with 'object[["AH121952"]]'
AH121952 is the accession number for Drosophila’s data!
Grab the organism database using the given accession number
org_db <- ah[["AH121952"]]
Let’s make some smaller dataframes. One with all the DEGs, one with the up-regulated* DEGs, and a final one with the down-regulated* DEGs. Remember, this is only for ONE pairwise comparison, which in this case is Maine’s 29C versus 21C samples.
sig_degs <- res_df %>% filter(diffexpressed != "NOT")
only_up_degs <- res_df %>% filter(diffexpressed == "UP")
only_down_degs <- res_df %>% filter(diffexpressed == "DOWN")
We truthfully, just need the gene names from each of these tables. However, if you recall from class, we need to know ALL the gene names too for our comparisons. This way we can determine if any given term is enriched relative to the “unvierse” of Drosophila’s genes and gene ontologies!
all_gene_names <- c(res_df$gene)
sig_deg_names <- c(sig_degs$gene)
sig_up_names <- c(only_up_degs$gene)
sig_down_names <- c(only_down_degs$gene)
You can see that I try to be NOT-creative with the naming. I recommend keeping it as straightforward as you can for yourself.
While we created our database of gene names from the GTF file originally from NCBI’s database, the gene names are really from FlyBase This is a standalone database that hosts the most up to date fly-related datasets and has its own naming. In fact, our gene names all start with Dmel_CG##### and we need to trim off the Dmel_ part. The rest are the same identifiers that FlyBase uses, which our organismal database is setup for too.
clean_sig_deg_names <- unlist(lapply(sig_deg_names, function(x) gsub("Dmel_", "", x)))
clean_uni_names <- unlist(lapply(all_gene_names, function(x) gsub("Dmel_", "", x)))
clean_sig_up_names <- unlist(lapply(sig_up_names, function(x) gsub("Dmel_", "", x)))
clean_sig_down_names <- unlist(lapply(sig_down_names, function(x) gsub("Dmel_", "", x)))
Great! Our names for the genes are clean now! We can figure out the functional enrichment patterns in our dataset!
ego <- enrichGO(
 gene = clean_sig_deg_names,
 universe = clean_uni_names,
 OrgDb = org_db,
 keyType = "FLYBASECG", # adjust keyType based on your input IDs
 ont = "BP", # BP: Biological Process, MF: Molecular Function, CC: Cellular Component, ALL: get all of them!
 pAdjustMethod = "BH",
 qvalueCutoff = 0.05,
 readable = TRUE)
Again, there is a lot in this command and it’s important to break it down.

gene =: this is your set of “clean” query genes. This can be JUST the up-regulated genes or all the deg genes.
unverse =: names of all the genes in the organism’s “universe”
OrgDB =: the organismal database from AnnotationHub
keyType =: where the names come from. NOTE: I will help you with this if you need it!
ont =: Gene ontology group
pAdjustMethod = “BH”: method for adjusting p-values for multiple comprisons (Benjamini-Hochberg method)
qvalueCutoff = 0.05: like a p-value but emphasizes false discovery rate
readable = TRUE: make the outputs readable!

Let’s make the dotplot to check out the enrichment!
dotplot(ego, showCategory=50)
Let’s stop for a moment. This plot is showing us the GO terms enriched in our differential gene expression data. They are NOT showing us those that are specifically up-regulated or down-regulated.
Repeat Steps 8 & 9, with the significantly up-regulated and down-regulated gene sets and see what you get!
I recommend updating the ego variable to something specific to the up/down regulated genes. I like to use: sig_up_ego and sig_down_ego, so I can quickly call on these plots without having to run any additional analyses.
I find these fascinating!
Before we move on, you can save the results for ALL of these data.
goa_summary <- data.frame(ego)
up_goa_summary <- data.frame(sig_up_ego)
down_goa_summary <- data.frame(sig_down_ego)

write.csv(goa_summary, file.path(dir, "Maine_21C_29C.All_DEGs.GOEnrichment.csv"))
write.csv(up_goa_summary, file.path(dir, "Maine_21C_29C.UpReg_DEGs.GOEnrichment.csv"))
write.csv(up_goa_summary, file.path(dir, "Maine_21C_29C.DownReg_DEGs.GOEnrichment.csv"))
Lastly, the final plot we are going to make is a bit weird. It is a network plot, but instead of showing interactions, it makes networks of genes with similar “functions” based on GO-term similarity. I think they look really interesting and can be informative (they are not always helpful).
ego_sim <- enrichplot::pairwise_termsim(ego)
emapplot(ego_sim, showCategory = 50)
When looking at these terms, it is not very clear how they correspond to heat stress. It may be that exploring the enrichment at the level of “Biological Process” is too broad. You should explore the enrichment with another GO term “level”

And that’s it! We will talk about natural follow up steps that are online in the lab itself. It is critical to mention that you should use these guided labs as an outline of how to do differential gene expression analyses. There are so many other considerations outside the scope of this lab to consider, but the goal is to “break through” that initial barrier! As someone that loves biochemistry, I like to think of the class as giving you the “activation energy” to catalyze your own learning :)

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Before we get started
All of the labs for this course will be in QuartoMD format like this. You will be required to copy these to your own personal account and should be updating them! Your only formal grades for this course are based on the semester project. These guided-labs are there to help you build your familiarity with creating documentation, managing, data, reporting, and with all sorts of coding and scripting.
Update and add things as you see fit! The more effort you place here, the more useful this will be for you!
At times, I will include blocks to highlight snippets of code and/or get you to pause and think!






Note



There will be some questions in blue that you can answer.


Some commands/instructions will have the potential to set you back, and require some deeper thought and/or carefulness.






Caution



This will highlight things that may need a bit of caution before you proceed.
This can include steps that may take a bit of time, or dangerous coding commands (e.g., those that remove all the files…)








Warning



Sometimes, it may just be a simple ‘warning’.


The first few weeks of the lab will focus on getting you comfortable with the command-line, before we move into diverse analyses, including differential gene expression and population genomics. This will include step-by-step instructions using our examplar data sets.
My goal is for you to feel comfortable enough to repeat the analyses on the data set of your choice!

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
W&M’s HPC server
If you are using your own computer and want to access the HPC from off-campus, then you will need to download the W&M VPN client. See this vpn installation link for instructions. If you are connected to the W&M Wi-Fi you will not need to connect to the VPN.
Once you are conneced to the W&M VPN, or using the W&M Wi-Fi, you will need to ssh into one of the sciclone’s subclusters. SciClone is comprised of many different servers (subclusters), each with their own unique set of resources (i.e., high powered CPU’s but low RAM). For most of the lab, we will be using bora.
If using your own computer and you run into issues accessing the HPC, ask me for help if needed!

Overview of the UNIX operating system and directory structure

The core structure of Unix directories follows a hierarchical tree-like organization. The root directory serves as the top-level directory, and all other directories and files are organized beneath it
When you first connect to the server, you will be in your home directory by default.
Keep this structure in mind when you’re navigating through directories, especially once we start up/downloading data to your personal computers.
If you ever get confused where you are you can return to the home directory using cd

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Connecting to bora.sciclone.wm.edu
For both PCs and Macs, I recommend using the terminal to access SciClone.

Open the Terminal software
Connect to the remote server using ssh with your username:






SSH into Bora



ssh cwwang@bora.sciclone.wm.edu

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
HPC Navigation
Moving around the HPC uses common UNIX commands (I will provide a link to a useful cheatsheet).
When you first log in, you are interacting the HPC’s head-node (we will talk about this in class!). Additionally, the location where you first “land” onto the HPC is not where you will work!
Before we do too much, let’s use some basic commands to see what is in our current folder, move around, and check where we are:

It may be kind of weird to think like this, but the parts of your laptop that you interact with really are just graphical representations of folders (directories). This is no different on the HPC! We can see the contents of this directory really easily.
ls
You should see a couple big directories, including scr10, scr20, scr30. These are the “scratch” spaces, which is our playground!






Storage Limitations



Do not store files outside of scr10 for this lab. Additionally, do not use scr10 as a semi-permanent storage space! It is purged every few months, so please treat it like a shared kitchen and make sure we clean up after ourselves when we can!


Let’s move into scr10, which is where we will do most of our work
cd scr10
It can be easy to get lost on the HPC! Thankfully, we have the best unix command ever: pwd
pwd






pwd is your Friend!



The output of pwd is the PATH to your current location. Each / marks a different directory, so you can see exactly where you are.
This is referred to as the absolute PATH, which is just like having exact GPS coordinates for where you are!


If you ever get lost, and this will happen, simply using cd will bring you back to your home directory
While we are here, let’s make a folder the lab too
mkdir Biol404L
Move into the new folder you made!






In case you get stumped





Use the cd command to move into your folder!
cd Biol404L



Use ls and pwd to see what is inside this folder and where you are on the HPC!
Move back to your home directory






In case you get stumped





Use the cd by itself to move to your home directory!
cd



Soon we will be done moving around for a little bit, just a few more to do! Let’s move directly into our Biol404L directory, then use pwd to check! bash     cd scr10/Biol404L     pwd You made it!
We can also move “backwards” to a less “nested” folder. We can use .. to navigate back a directory relative to where we are. Let’s try it out and see what it looks like! bash     cd ..     pwd
Move back into your Biol404L folder (see the prior commands/steps if you need help, before asking me or a neighbor)
Let’s move “backwards” two times at once! bash     cd ../..






Did you notice?





To move back one directory, we use ... However, to move back two directories, we have to put a ‘/’ in the middle!
You can do this as many times as needed, although it can get confusing…



Where are you now? How would you check? using pwd
If you feel comfortable, make sure to move back into the Biol404L folder.
One last task before we continue! Make a new directory called Slurm_Scripts then move into it!






In case you get stumped





You can use the mkdir command!
mkdir Slurm_Scripts
cd Slurm_Scripts




Great! You are now on your way to becoming a UNIX navigation expert.

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Dealing with Containers
This next section will combine a fair bit of commands, which will become more familiar as you work in this lab. You are not expected to be an expert right away!

Loading Modules (Software)
The HPC has quite a lot of software already installed on it. This varies by with subclusters you are working with (remember we are working on bora).






Want to see the available software





If you do, then run the following command:
module avail



We do want to use containers in this lab. To do so, we will be using Anaconda and BioConda.

Load the miniforge module
module load miniforge3/24.9.2-0
Let’s see what modules are loaded already
module avail






What do you see?





You should notice that two pieces of software are highlighted!
SLURM and Miniforge3!



Miniforge3 is our Anaconda software. However, it does not natively connect or know where to find bioinformatic packages. Most of those are available through BioConda.
We will follow the BioConda setup instructions for Conda that are found on their website.
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict

Now we are almost ready to install software! Woohoo!
It is worth noting that conda refers to their “containers” as environments. For our purposes, this is the same thing, so do not be alarmed!

title: Accessing W&M’s HPC
text:
Submitting HPC Jobs
In this part we will set up a job submission script. These are important to understand as we will be using them throughout the lab course.
I have placed a template of one below (I will break down what each part means!):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH -t 1:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G
You can change the job name, the -t refers to parallelizing tasks or doing many things at the same time, and the bottom line controls how much memory this task will take up.
It is nice to keep your job submission scripts together, staying organized is KEY!


Making our first job-submission-script
We will actually be submitting a job to make our container and install some software! The easiest option is to use an existing text editor in the terminal, pico

Open a new file, nano prep_conda_env.sh, with pico Your screen should be empty!
Copy and paste the template for our job submission that was found in the last section
To “write” the file quickly (equivalent of saving), press ctl+o keys at the same time and hit enter
Now, using your arrow keys, please replace some-job-name with env-prep and “write” the file again
Great, we are ready to add our command! We will create a new environment, called sra_prep. In it we will install several pieces of software:

sra-tools: this makes it easy to download raw data from NCBI’s SRA repository
ncbi-datasets-cli: makes it easy to access genomes from NCBI’s GenBank and RefSeq
parallel-fastq-dump: speeds up the initial unpacking of SRA data
fastp: quality trimming tool (also provides lovely QC outputs!)

Add the following to your script:
conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools parallel-fastq-dump fastp -y
Make sure to save!
Check your script (below)






Working Submission Script





#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=some-job-name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH -t 1:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G

conda create -n sra_prep ncbi-datasets-cli sra-tools fastp parallel-fastq-dump -y



Exit the pico editor with ctl+x
Submitting the job to run is incredibly easy! You will just use sbatch
sbatch prep_conda_env.sh
Now we wait… You can track the progress in the queue! Very useful!
squeue --m
Above will show only your jobs, whereas the code below will show *all the jobs
squeue
head slurm-[insert JOBID #].out will show the first 10 jobs running rn

tail slurm-[insert JOBID #].out will show the last 10 jobs

Once this is finished, you will need to make one more container! Updating the prep_conda_env.sh script, you will need to:


create a new container called txpt_quant
install salmon
install star

Make sure this is run before we meet next!

Once your job is finished, activate your container! bash     conda activate sra_prep If it works, you will see (sra_prep) on the left-hand side of the terminal!
Look at the fastp help message and all its options (so many) bash     fastp -h
Using -h with most tools will bring up usage information along with all their options. It is a lazy nice way to make to sure that the software is installed!
To exit the HPC, simply press ctl+d at the same time! You should see something like: Connection to bora.sciclone.wm.edu closed.

Disconnecting from the HPC is safe to do any time that a job is running or queued!
In fact, that is the advantage of the HPC! You can queue some work then do something else (nap, eat some cookies, compose a bioinformatics sonnet, etc)
You made it! Huzzah!

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Unpacking SRA datasets
If you were curious and used ls to peek into those newly created folders, you would have seen a file ending in .sra. This is the packed (compressed) raw data!
We need to unpack it using the tool parallel-fastq-dump.
Below, is a walkthrough of one way to do this. It is a bit involved, but it will make it easy to link the file to the existing metadata!
You should repeat the following steps for each file

Make a copy of last week’s slurm script and rename it sra_fastq_dump.sh
cp ../Slurm_Scripts/prep_conda_env.sh ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_fastq_dump.sh
Make some extra edits to this file!

update the job-name
update the --ntasks value to 8
delete the old command

Now we will add the command to run parallel-fastq-dump
parallel-fastq-dump --split-files \
     --gzip \
     --threads 8 \
     -s SRR1576457 \
     -O Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1
Here is a breakdown of the command:

--split-files: separate the file into forward and reverse reads (the data are paired-end!)
--gzip: these raw fastq files can be big, so we will keep them compressed
--threads 8: tells the HPC to multi-task on this job, splitting the job into 8 pieces to speed it up
-s SRR#: tells the tool which dataset we want to process
-O NAME: the name we want the output folder to be. It is typically nice to include the metadata and/or the SRR accession (or both)

Using sbatch, submit the job!
Repeat for the other datasets that have FINISHED downloading. Use squeue --m to check that the files you are trying to unpack have finished downloading!
As before, it is up to you to unpack the rest of the datasets during our time in lab (or outside if that’s easier). So long as one of the sequencing runs is downloaded and unpacked, you can move on to the last section, which is trimming and the quality checking!

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Trimming raw SRA datasets
If you were curious and used ls to peek into those newly created folders, you would have seen a file ending in .sra. This is the packed (compressed) raw data!
We need to unpack it using the tool parallel-fastq-dump.
Below, is a walkthrough of one way to do this. It is a bit involved, but it will make it easy to link the file to the existing metadata!
You should repeat the following steps for each file

Make a copy of the sra_fastq_dump.sh slurm script and rename it sra_fastq_trim.sh






In case you get stumped





cp ../Slurm_Scripts/prep_conda_env.sh ../Slurm_Scripts/sra_fastq_trim.sh



You will need to edit the newly copied script, sra_fastq_trim.sh. As the prior script already was set up for multi-threading (--ntasks=8), the only change is to replace the prior command with one for our read-trimming tool, fastp.
The command is below, followed by a breakdown of the options. The below command is written for just one file, so you will need to adjust this!
fastp \
     -i Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1/SRR1576457_1.fastq.gz \
     -I Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1/SRR1576457_2.fastq.gz \
     -o Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -O Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
     -h Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.html \
     -R "Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1 Report" \
     -q 20  \
     -l 80 \
     -w 8 \
     -r
Here is a breakdown of the command:

-i: PATH to your forward reads
-I: PATH to your reverse reads
-o: what to name your trimmed forward reads
-O: what to name your trimmed reverse reads
-h: what to name the output quality score html file
-R: the report name to add to the output quality score html file
-q: minimum Phred quality score to use for read trimming
-l: minimum read length to keep a read following trimming
-w: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as --ntasks)
-r: perform the per-base trimming starting on the right side of the read

Using sbatch, submit the job!
Repeat for the other datasets that have FINISHED unpacking with parallel-fastq-dump. Use squeue --m to check that the files you are trying to unpack have finished downloading!

title: Working with SRA Data
text:
Cleaning up after ourselves
By now, you will have tons of files, all sitting inside your raw_read_prep folder. We do need to make sure to clean-up after ourselves on the HPC, as we have many “intermediate” files, which take up a reasonably large amount of space.
To do our cleanup, we will be using a dangerous command, rm. What makes this command so dangerous is that it removes the files/folders permanently. This is like moving a file to your trash on your computer and tossing the trash out at the same time.
Take your time when doing this! We will remove files little bit by little bit.

Running and submitting jobs to SLURM will generate a ton of “slurm.out” files. These are logs from the HPC and the tool(s) you used. Typically, you won’t need these for very long, outside of handling errors.
We can remove all of these in one step!






Removing slurm logs



rm slurm-*.out


rm followed by a file, will remove the file. You can also use the wildcard character, *. In the example above, the way this is put in the command effectively tells the computer “remove anything that startswith slurm- and ends with .out”
Make sure to remove all the files that end with .json as we do not need these!






Removing slurm logs



rm *.json


This step is for any sequencing runs that have been fully processed, which includes downloading, unpacking, trimming. We will start by removing each of the intermediate folders, one at a time. It is okay to do this slowly and carefully, as you don’t want to need to do the processing over again.
Below is the command to remove just one of the folders from the initial SRR downloading






Removing Folders



rm -rf SRR1576457


You can combine this with the wildcard to remove all of the SRR folders, but you need to be very certain you have “unpacked” them!
You can also use that command to remove any folders, but again, please be cautious!
